# Differential expression with DESeq2 and edgeR {#sec-de} We now ask which genes change in expression when TDP-43 is knocked down. The main tool is DESeq2 [@love2014]; edgeR's quasi-likelihood pipeline [@robinson2010; @chen2016] serves as a second method that is often preferred for small sample sizes. At the end we look at what happens if the batch had not been recorded, using surrogate variable analysis [@leek2014]. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/helpers.R") suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(DESeq2) library(edgeR) library(sva) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) }) fmt_p <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1) ``` ::: ## The comparison From @sec-design and @sec-qc we take three decisions: - **Samples**: TDP-43 siRNA (n = 6) versus scramble siRNA (n = 6). - **Model**: `~ batch + condition`, because batch is the largest source of variation and is balanced across groups. - **Reference level**: scramble, so that positive log2 fold changes mean *higher in the knockdown*. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rse <- load_counts_rse() rse <- rse[, rse$sirna %in% c("scramble", "TDP43")] rse$condition <- droplevels(rse$sirna) rse$batch <- droplevels(rse$batch) table(condition = rse$condition, batch = rse$batch) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> batch #> condition B1 B2 #> scramble 2 4 #> TDP43 2 4 ``` ::: ::: ## Setting the reference level explicitly R orders factor levels alphabetically unless told otherwise. Here that would happen to give the right answer ("scramble" before "TDP43"), but relying on alphabetical order is fragile: name the groups "WT" and "KD" and the knockdown silently becomes the reference, flipping the sign of every fold change. We therefore always set the reference with `relevel()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rse$condition <- relevel(factor(rse$condition), ref = "scramble") levels(rse$condition) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "scramble" "TDP43" ``` ::: ::: ## Filtering low counts Genes with very few reads carry almost no information and add to the multiple-testing burden. Our rule: **at least 10 counts in at least as many samples as the smallest group** (here 6). The rule ignores the group labels, so it cannot bias the test towards one group. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds <- DESeqDataSet(rse, design = ~ batch + condition) min_group <- min(table(dds$condition)) keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= min_group dds <- dds[keep, ] c(smallest_group = min_group, genes_tested = nrow(dds)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> smallest_group genes_tested #> 6 20683 ``` ::: ::: ## Fitting the model `DESeq()` estimates size factors (library size normalisation), fits one dispersion per gene with shrinkage towards a trend, and fits a negative binomial GLM for each gene. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds <- DESeq(dds) resultsNames(dds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "Intercept" "batch_B2_vs_B1" #> [3] "condition_TDP43_vs_scramble" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plotDispEsts(dds) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Dispersion estimates. Black: per-gene estimates; red: fitted trend; blue: final shrunken estimates. Circled points are outliers kept at their own estimate.](05-differential-expression_files/figure-html/fig-dispersion-1.png){#fig-dispersion fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The dispersion plot is a quick health check: estimates should scatter around a smooth decreasing trend, as they do here. ## Results: raw and shrunken fold changes `results()` gives the maximum likelihood log2 fold change, its standard error, and a Wald test p-value adjusted for multiple testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg method (padj). For genes with few counts, the raw log2 fold change can be very large simply because of noise. `lfcShrink()` with the apeglm prior [@zhu2019] pulls noisy estimates towards zero while leaving well-supported large effects almost untouched. We use the **shrunken** values for ranking and plots, and keep the **raw** values in the table as well, in separate, clearly named columns. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} coef_name <- "condition_TDP43_vs_scramble" res <- results(dds, name = coef_name, alpha = DE_PADJ) res_shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = coef_name, type = "apeglm", quiet = TRUE) summary(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> out of 20683 with nonzero total read count #> adjusted p-value < 0.05 #> LFC > 0 (up) : 707, 3.4% #> LFC < 0 (down) : 728, 3.5% #> outliers [1] : 0, 0% #> low counts [2] : 401, 1.9% #> (mean count < 11) #> [1] see 'cooksCutoff' argument of ?results #> [2] see 'independentFiltering' argument of ?results ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} de <- data.frame( gene_id = rownames(res), symbol = rowData(dds)$gene_name, gene_type = rowData(dds)$gene_type, baseMean = res$baseMean, log2FC = res$log2FoldChange, # raw (MLE) lfcSE = res$lfcSE, # raw (MLE) log2FC_shrunk = res_shr$log2FoldChange, # apeglm lfcSE_shrunk = res_shr$lfcSE, # apeglm stat = res$stat, pvalue = res$pvalue, padj = res$padj ) |> arrange(padj) ``` ::: ## Calling differentially expressed genes Our predefined thresholds are **padj < 0.05** and **|log2FC| > 1**. We apply the fold change cut-off to the shrunken estimate, so that a gene cannot pass only because its raw fold change is inflated by noise. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} de <- de |> mutate(DE = case_when( !is.na(padj) & padj < DE_PADJ & log2FC_shrunk > DE_LFC ~ "up", !is.na(padj) & padj < DE_PADJ & log2FC_shrunk < -DE_LFC ~ "down", TRUE ~ "not significant")) table(de$DE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> down not significant up #> 23 20623 37 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} de |> filter(DE != "not significant") |> slice_head(n = 15) |> mutate(across(c(baseMean, log2FC, lfcSE, log2FC_shrunk, lfcSE_shrunk), \(x) round(x, 2)), across(c(pvalue, padj), fmt_p)) |> select(gene_id, symbol, baseMean, log2FC, lfcSE, log2FC_shrunk, pvalue, padj, DE) |> knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |gene_id |symbol | baseMean| log2FC| lfcSE| log2FC_shrunk|pvalue |padj |DE | |down | |ENSG00000126759.13 |CFP | 45.29| 1.47| 0.20| 1.41|7.6e-13 |3.5e-10 |up | |ENSG00000283265.1 |RP11-95M15.3 | 19.64| 2.07| 0.29| 1.99|1.5e-12 |6.4e-10 |up | ::: ::: Of the 1435 genes with padj < 0.05, only 60 also change more than two-fold. Most responses to a partial TDP-43 knockdown are modest, which is why the fold change threshold has to be fixed in advance: a slightly different cut-off would change the list a lot, and choosing it after seeing the result would make the list meaningless. *TARDBP* itself should be among the most significant genes, and it is. Next to it in the table are two other GENCODE v26 genes annotated on top of the *TARDBP* locus: RP4-635E18.9, whose exons overlap *TARDBP*, and RP4-635E18.8, just downstream of it. recount3 counts a read for every gene whose exons it covers, so genes that share sequence with the siRNA target drop together with it. They are not independent findings. *STMN2* is also strongly reduced, while *UNC13A* and *POLDIP3* do not change at the gene level. For *UNC13A* that is not evidence against a splicing effect; we come back to it in @sec-cryptic. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} de |> filter(symbol %in% c("TARDBP", "STMN2", "UNC13A", "POLDIP3")) |> mutate(across(c(baseMean, log2FC, log2FC_shrunk), \(x) round(x, 2)), across(c(pvalue, padj), fmt_p)) |> select(symbol, baseMean, log2FC, log2FC_shrunk, padj, DE) |> knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |symbol | baseMean| log2FC| log2FC_shrunk|padj |DE | |:-------|--------:|------:|-------------:|:-------|:---------------| |TARDBP | 1869.57| -1.35| -1.34|7.7e-79 |down | |STMN2 | 33311.09| -1.12| -1.11|3.7e-49 |down | |UNC13A | 3486.11| -0.18| -0.12|2.1e-01 |not significant | |POLDIP3 | 1812.23| 0.05| 0.05|4.7e-01 |not significant | ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## A formal test against a fold change threshold Filtering on |log2FC| after testing against zero is common practice, but the padj then refers to "any change", not to "a change larger than 2-fold". If you need the latter, DESeq2 can test it directly with `results(dds, lfcThreshold = 1)`. Here this gives 3 genes, compared with 60 from the filter approach. Report which approach you used. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} write.csv(de, "results/de_deseq2_TDP43_vs_scramble.csv", row.names = FALSE) saveRDS(dds, cache_path("dds_TDP43_vs_scramble.rds")) write.csv(as.data.frame(counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)) |> tibble::rownames_to_column("gene_id"), gzfile(cache_path("normalized_counts.csv.gz")), row.names = FALSE) ``` ::: The full table is saved as `results/de_deseq2_TDP43_vs_scramble.csv`. ## edgeR quasi-likelihood: a second opinion With only a handful of replicates per group, the quasi-likelihood (QL) F-test in edgeR is a good alternative: it accounts for the uncertainty in estimating each gene's dispersion and tends to be conservative. We use the same genes and the same design so that the two methods can be compared directly. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- DGEList(counts = counts(dds), samples = as.data.frame(colData(dds)[, c("condition", "batch")])) y <- normLibSizes(y) # TMM normalisation design <- model.matrix(~ batch + condition, data = y$samples) fit <- glmQLFit(y, design) qlf <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = "conditionTDP43") et <- topTags(qlf, n = Inf, sort.by = "none")$table edger <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(et), logFC = et$logFC, PValue = et$PValue, FDR = et$FDR) edger$DE <- with(edger, ifelse(FDR < DE_PADJ & abs(logFC) > DE_LFC, ifelse(logFC > 0, "up", "down"), "not significant")) table(edger$DE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> down not significant up #> 31 20601 51 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp <- inner_join(de, edger, by = "gene_id", suffix = c(".deseq2", ".edger")) sig_d <- cmp$gene_id[cmp$DE.deseq2 != "not significant"] sig_e <- cmp$gene_id[cmp$DE.edger != "not significant"] both <- intersect(sig_d, sig_e) data.frame( DESeq2_only = length(setdiff(sig_d, sig_e)), both = length(both), edgeR_only = length(setdiff(sig_e, sig_d)), same_direction_in_both = mean(sign(cmp$log2FC[cmp$gene_id %in% both]) == sign(cmp$logFC[cmp$gene_id %in% both])), spearman_logFC_all_genes = cor(cmp$log2FC, cmp$logFC, method = "spearman") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| DESeq2_only| both| edgeR_only| same_direction_in_both| spearman_logFC_all_genes| |-----------:|----:|----------:|----------------------:|------------------------:| | 6| 54| 28| 1| 0.9964249|
::: ::: Both methods call largely the same genes (54 shared, 6 DESeq2 only, 28 edgeR only), every shared gene changes in the same direction, and the fold changes of all tested genes are almost perfectly rank-correlated. edgeR calls more genes here mainly because we applied the fold change cut-off to the *shrunken* DESeq2 estimate but to the unshrunken edgeR estimate. Genes called by only one method sit close to a threshold in both; they are a reminder that a cut-off is a convention, not a property of the gene. ## What if the batch had not been recorded? Suppose the dates were missing from the metadata. PCA would still show two clusters of samples, but we would not know why. Surrogate variable analysis (svaseq) estimates hidden factors from the data, and these can be added to the model in place of the unknown batch. Two rules apply whenever you use it: 1. **Report the number of surrogate variables (SVs)** and how it was chosen. 2. **Report a sensitivity check**: how many genes pass the thresholds with and without the SVs, how many overlap, and whether the direction agrees. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds_nobatch <- DESeqDataSet(rse[rownames(dds), ], design = ~ condition) dds_nobatch <- estimateSizeFactors(dds_nobatch) norm_counts <- counts(dds_nobatch, normalized = TRUE) mod <- model.matrix(~ condition, colData(dds_nobatch)) mod0 <- model.matrix(~ 1, colData(dds_nobatch)) n_sv <- num.sv(log2(norm_counts + 1), mod, method = "be", seed = 1) set.seed(1) sv <- svaseq(norm_counts, mod, mod0, n.sv = n_sv)$sv ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Number of significant surrogate variables is: 3 #> Iteration (out of 5 ):1 2 3 4 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} colnames(sv) <- paste0("SV", seq_len(ncol(sv))) n_sv ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: The permutation-based method ("be") suggests 3 surrogate variable(s). Does the first one recover the batch we hid? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} round(cor(sv, as.numeric(dds_nobatch$batch == "B2")), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [,1] #> SV1 -0.98 #> SV2 -0.18 #> SV3 0.03 ``` ::: ::: Now fit three models on the same genes and compare them. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_calls <- function(d) { d <- DESeq(d, quiet = TRUE) cf <- "condition_TDP43_vs_scramble" r <- results(d, name = cf, alpha = DE_PADJ) s <- lfcShrink(d, coef = cf, type = "apeglm", quiet = TRUE) data.frame(gene_id = rownames(r), lfc = s$log2FoldChange, padj = r$padj, sig = !is.na(r$padj) & r$padj < DE_PADJ & abs(s$log2FoldChange) > DE_LFC) } colData(dds_nobatch) <- cbind(colData(dds_nobatch), sv) sv_formula <- as.formula(paste("~", paste(colnames(sv), collapse = " + "), "+ condition")) models <- list( batch_known = de |> transmute(gene_id, lfc = log2FC_shrunk, padj, sig = DE != "not significant"), no_adjustment = fit_calls(DESeqDataSet(rse[rownames(dds), ], design = ~ condition)), svaseq = fit_calls(DESeqDataSet(SummarizedExperiment( assays = list(counts = counts(dds_nobatch)), colData = colData(dds_nobatch)), design = sv_formula)) ) ref <- models$batch_known sens <- lapply(names(models), function(m) { x <- inner_join(ref, models[[m]], by = "gene_id", suffix = c(".ref", ".m")) shared <- x$sig.ref & x$sig.m data.frame(model = m, genes_passing = sum(x$sig.m), overlap_with_batch_model = sum(shared), same_direction = if (any(shared)) mean(sign(x$lfc.ref[shared]) == sign(x$lfc.m[shared])) else NA) }) do.call(rbind, sens) |> knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |model | genes_passing| overlap_with_batch_model| same_direction| |:-------------|-------------:|------------------------:|--------------:| |batch_known | 60| 60| 1| |no_adjustment | 32| 32| 1| |svaseq | 43| 34| 1| ::: ::: How to read this table: - **no_adjustment** ignores the batch completely. Because batch was the largest source of variation, leaving it out inflates the residual variance, so only 32 genes pass, all of them also found by the batch model. - **svaseq** used 3 surrogate variables. The first one is almost the hidden batch (correlation -0.98). It finds 43 genes, of which 34 are shared with the known-batch model, all with the same direction. These three numbers (genes passing, overlap, direction agreement) are the sensitivity check you report. - The 9 genes found only with SVs are not "extra discoveries". They show that the SVs also absorb some variation that is not batch, which changes the result at the margin. ::: {.callout-warning} ## When not to use SVA If the batch is known, model it directly, as we did. Surrogate variables can absorb part of the biological signal when the hidden factor is correlated with the condition, and they make the model harder to explain. SVA is a tool for unknown structure, not a replacement for recording your batches. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check your understanding 1. What would change in the results table if you forgot `relevel()` and the groups were named "WT" and "KD"? 2. Why do we apply the |log2FC| cut-off to the shrunken rather than the raw fold change? 3. The filter keeps genes with at least 10 counts in at least 6 samples. Why 6, and why is this filter not biased towards either group? 4. You used svaseq and found 3 SVs. What else must you report? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Answers 1. "KD" sorts before "WT", so the knockdown would become the reference and every log2 fold change would flip sign, with no warning. `relevel()` removes the dependency on spelling. 2. Raw fold changes of low-count genes are noisy and can be large by chance. Shrinkage keeps large, well-supported effects and pulls noisy ones towards zero, so the cut-off selects genes with reliable large effects. 3. 6 is the size of the smallest group, so a gene expressed in only one group can still pass. The rule does not look at group labels, so it is independent of the test statistic under the null hypothesis. 4. How the number was chosen, and a sensitivity analysis: genes passing with and without SVs, their overlap, and the direction agreement. ::: :::
